title: Transfer: Network Delay Time
oneLiner: A signal leaves one node and travels along directed, timed links. How long until every node has it? Dijkstra, then one more question about its answer.
keyTakeaway: A signal spreading from k reaches each node first along that node's shortest path, so every arrival time is a Dijkstra distance. Everyone has the signal once the slowest arrival happens: the answer is the largest distance, or -1 if any node is never reached.
explanation:
This follows Dijkstra's Shortest Path with the problem dressed differently. A network has n nodes numbered 0 to n - 1. times[i] = [u, v, w] means a signal sent from u reaches v after w time units; links are one way, and there may be several links between the same two nodes. A signal starts at node k at time 0 and every node forwards it along all its links the moment it arrives. Return the time at which every node has received it, or -1 if some node never does.

Two things changed from the parent lesson. The graph comes as a list of directed edges, so you build the adjacency list yourself (an edge u -> v goes only into u's list). And the answer isn't the distance array but one number derived from it.

When does node v first get the signal? The signal tries every route at once, so v hears it at the length of its fastest route from k: exactly dist[v] from Dijkstra. All nodes have it once the last of them hears it, at max(dist). If some dist is still infinity, that node is unreachable and the answer is -1.

So: build adj from times, run Dijkstra from k with a priority queue of (distance, node), skip stale entries, relax edges, then take the maximum. Parallel edges need no special care, since relaxing picks the cheaper one. With E links and V = n nodes it is O((V + E) log V) time and O(V + E) space, as in the parent lesson.

The visualization runs n = 5, k = 0 over six links and shows dist after each node is finalized; "inf" means not reached yet.

Explain why the same idea works: before you move on, write two or three sentences on why this is Dijkstra in disguise. Why is the time a node first hears the signal the same as its shortest path distance, why is the answer the maximum and not the sum, and what does an unreachable node do to it?

visualizationSteps.message: Node 0 hears the signal at time 0 (the smallest unfinished distance). Relax its links: dist[1] = 4, dist[2] = 1.
Node 2 hears the signal at time 1 (the smallest unfinished distance). Relax its links: dist[1] = 3, dist[3] = 6.
Node 1 hears the signal at time 3 (the smallest unfinished distance). Relax its links: dist[3] = 4.
Node 3 hears the signal at time 4 (the smallest unfinished distance). Relax its links: dist[4] = 7.
Node 4 hears the signal at time 7. Its links offer nothing faster.
Every node is reached. The last one hears it at time 7, so the answer is 7.

recognitionSignals: Something spreads from one source along weighted links (signal, rumour, infection, water) and the question is when the last place is reached.
Non-negative travel times and "how long until everyone", which is the largest of the shortest distances.
gotchas: The links are directed: add u -> v only, not v -> u.
Return -1 if any node is unreachable; the maximum of the reachable distances alone is wrong.
The answer is the largest shortest distance, not the sum of the edge times on some spanning tree.
confusableWith: Graphs: Dijkstra's Shortest Path returns every distance from the source; this is the same computation followed by one max over the result.
Minimum spanning tree also picks cheap edges, but it minimises the total edge weight, not how long the farthest node waits.

complexity.note: Building the adjacency list is O(V + E). Dijkstra with lazy deletion pushes at most E + 1 entries, each push or pop O(log E) = O(log V), and the final max is O(V). Space is the adjacency list plus dist and up to E queue entries.
